common_name: Savoy Ace Cabbage (AAS-Winning Crinkled-Leaf Savoy Cabbage)

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Savoy Ace is an All-America Selections winner bred for reliable heading and the tender, crinkled leaves characteristic of savoy-type cabbage.

directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, spacing plants to allow full head development. Savoy Ace, an All-America Selections winner, forms attractive, deeply crinkled, blue-green leaves wrapped into a dense, tender head, with the savoy type's characteristically milder flavor and more tender texture compared with smooth-leaf cabbage, making it excellent for salads as well as cooked dishes. It heads reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions that can cause other savoy cabbages to form loose or split heads. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Ruby Perfection is an All-America Selections winner bred for uniform, dense red heads and reliable performance.

directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop. Ruby Perfection, an All-America Selections winner, forms dense, round, deep reddish-purple heads that hold their color and quality well, both in the garden and in storage, on a compact plant bred for uniform heading and dependable performance across varying growing conditions. Its rich color makes it a striking addition to salads, slaws, and pickled preparations in addition to standard cooked use. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm and dense to the touch.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production

common_name: Simpson Elite Lettuce (AAS-Winning Improved Black Seeded Simpson)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Simpson Elite is an All-America Selections winner bred as an improved version of the classic Black Seeded Simpson, with better bolt resistance.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Simpson Elite, an All-America Selections winner, improves on the classic heirloom Black Seeded Simpson looseleaf lettuce with notably better resistance to bolting in warm weather, extending the harvest window later into spring and giving Gulf South gardeners more usable growing time before summer heat sets in. It forms loose, tender, light green frilled leaves ready for cut-and-come-again harvest within weeks of sowing. Harvest outer leaves as needed while the center continues to produce, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest weeks of the season to further delay bolting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Slo-Bolt is a classic looseleaf lettuce bred specifically to resist bolting and bitterness longer than most lettuce as weather warms.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Slo-Bolt lives up to its name as one of the most heat-resistant looseleaf lettuces available, holding good flavor and resisting the bitterness and premature flowering that end the harvest of most lettuce varieties once temperatures climb, making it a favorite for extending the spring lettuce season deeper into the Gulf South's warm months. It produces medium green, slightly frilled leaves in a loose, open rosette well suited to cut-and-come-again harvest. Pick outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing, and provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to push the harvest window even further.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, forms small, round, golf-ball-sized roots that mature quickly and grow well even in shallow or heavy, rocky soil unsuited to long-rooted carrot varieties.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up. Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, produces small, round, sweet roots about the size of a golf ball rather than the long tapered shape of standard carrots, making it uniquely well suited to shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils where long-rooted carrots often grow forked or stunted, as well as to container growing. Its quick maturity and compact size also make it a fun, kid-friendly carrot for small gardens. Harvest as soon as roots reach full size, since round carrots can become woody if left in the ground too long, and keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender roots.
